items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: Trumbau. Frankie Trumbau, to me, I think that he was really great. ... Even to when he was playing with Bix, Bix was so strong, you see, that he overshadowed anyone and everyone.

ctx.x: Yeah, and you remember every solo. Pretty near. Very few of them. That's the most fantastic thing. And he remembers Trumbau by solos, too.

Trumbau. Frankie Trumbau, to me, I think that he was really great. I mean, to me, he is very, very underrated. Uh-huh. Even to when he was playing with Bix, Bix was so strong, you see, that he overshadowed anyone and everyone. And, of course, I think that really Trumbau did a lot to enhance him when they were playing together. Uh-huh. Because it seemed as though that Trumbau knew every move that he made. Uh-huh. There was nothing that Bix ever did that you wouldn't hear Trumbau right along with him. And it sounds…
Beautiful, beautiful combination. And I think they originated the so-called chase choruses in some of those numbers where back and forth they would answer each other.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: we were standing up talking to Bix and Frankie Trumbauer.

ctx.x: I want to get back to Dixon in the mist. How did he play on the piano? Did he play more or less legitimately or did he have unusual things?

Well you know, Dixon's piano playing was really amazing because in listening to Dixon's Bix playing piano, I can never really tie in his trumpet with the piano. I don't know if it ever struck you that way, Dick, but listening to his trumpet, it sounds like it's an entirely different phase than his piano playing. His piano sounds so different that it was rhythmical with really sort of modern chords and yet there was the old time flavor along with it. It's just a hard thing to explain, his piano playing. You know,…
Did you ever hear Brownlee's band? Norman Brownlee?
